subject: Physics
topic: Optics III — total internal reflection, optical fibre, critical angle
description: Total internal reflection, critical angle, optical fibre working principle, refractive index relationship, applications.

questions.stem: Total Internal Reflection (TIR) occurs when light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the:

options.option_text: Critical angle (θc — beyond this, no refraction occurs)
Brewster angle (angle for complete polarisation)
Normal angle (90° to the surface — not a threshold)
Refraction angle (angle of refracted ray, not incident)

questions.explanation: TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION (TIR): When light travels from DENSER (higher n) → RARER (lower n) medium and angle of incidence > CRITICAL ANGLE (θc), all light is reflected back — no refraction occurs. TWO CONDITIONS for TIR: (1) Light must go from denser to rarer. (2) Angle of incidence must exceed θc. CRITICAL ANGLE formula: sin(θc) = n₂/n₁ (where n₁ = denser medium, n₂ = rarer). For glass-air interface (n_glass ≈ 1.5, n_air = 1): sin(θc) = 1/1.5 = 2/3 → θc ≈ 42°. BREWSTER ANGLE: angle at which reflected light is fully polarised (different phenomenon — not TIR). APPLICATIONS of TIR: (1) OPTICAL FIBRES — data transmission (internet, endoscopes). (2) DIAMOND BRILLIANCE — high refractive index (2.42) → θc ≈ 24° → multiple TIRs → sparkling. (3) MIRAGE — hot air above road is rarer; light bends and undergoes TIR → image of sky appears on road. (4) PERISCOPE prisms — 45° prism deflects light 90° via TIR. PYQ FREQUENCY: TIR and critical angle appear in SSC CGL, NDA, UPSC Prelims Physics 1-2× per cycle. MEMORY AID: TIR = 'Total Inner Reflection = light is Totally Trapped Inside the Rarer-to-Denser transition.'

questions.stem: An optical fibre carries data using total internal reflection. The light signal travels through the:

options.option_text: Core (denser inner layer) with the cladding (rarer outer layer) ensuring TIR
Cladding (outer layer) while the core prevents leakage (not this)
Buffer coating (protective layer) by repeated reflections (not this)
Air gap between core and cladding where refractive index is zero

questions.explanation: OPTICAL FIBRE STRUCTURE (from inside out): (1) CORE — denser glass/silica (higher refractive index, typically 1.5). (2) CLADDING — rarer glass (lower refractive index, ~1.46). (3) BUFFER COATING — plastic protective layer (no optical role). WORKING: Light enters the CORE at a small angle → hits the core-cladding interface at angle > θc → TIR → light zigzags through the CORE all the way to the other end without significant energy loss. KEY PRINCIPLE: The DENSER medium (core) is where light travels; the RARER medium (cladding) acts as a mirror wall via TIR. ADVANTAGES over copper wire: (1) Higher bandwidth (can carry more data). (2) No electromagnetic interference. (3) Lower signal loss over long distances. (4) Lighter and thinner cables. APPLICATIONS: Internet backbone cables (undersea fibre optic cables), endoscopy (medical — sees inside body), decorative lighting, sensing. UPSC ANGLE: Submarine cable landings in India (Chennai, Mumbai) connect to global internet. India's BharatNet project uses optical fibre to connect gram panchayats. PYQ FREQUENCY: optical fibre in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims Science/Tech, IBPS PO GA 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: A mirage on a hot road is explained by total internal reflection. Which layer of air acts as the denser medium in this phenomenon?

options.option_text: Cooler upper air (higher density → higher refractive index)
Hot lower air (lower density → actually rarer medium)
The road surface itself (solid — not where refraction happens)
Both layers equally (mirage requires uniform density)

questions.explanation: MIRAGE PHYSICS: On a hot day, air near the road is HOT → LOW DENSITY → LOWER refractive index (rarer). Air above is COOLER → HIGHER DENSITY → HIGHER refractive index (denser). Light from the sky travels downward from denser (cooler) air toward rarer (hot) air. As the angle of incidence increases beyond critical angle, TIR occurs → light bends back upward. The observer's eye receives light that seems to come from the road surface → appears like water (a mirage). KEY SCIENCE: (1) Rarer medium = hot low-density air near road. (2) Denser medium = cool high-density air above. (3) Light travels from denser → rarer → TIR. DESERT MIRAGES (superior mirage): cold land, warm air above → opposite — image appears above the actual object. UPSC ANGLE: atmospheric optics including mirages, looming, sinking appear in UPSC Science & Tech. Real-world consequence: road surface appears wet in summer heat → dangerous optical illusion for drivers. PYQ FREQUENCY: mirage and TIR in SSC CGL Tier 1, NDA Physics 1× per cycle. EXAM TRAP: students think hot air = denser — WRONG. Hot air is LESS dense (molecules spread out), giving lower refractive index.

questions.stem: The refractive index of diamond is approximately 2.42. Its critical angle with respect to air is closest to:

options.option_text: 42° (critical angle of glass — not diamond)
60° (too high for such a dense medium)
48° (inverse of sin rule misapplied)

questions.explanation: CRITICAL ANGLE formula: sin(θc) = n_rarer/n_denser = 1/n_diamond (since n_air = 1). sin(θc) = 1/2.42 ≈ 0.413 → θc ≈ sin⁻¹(0.413) ≈ 24.4° ≈ 24°. SIGNIFICANCE: Diamond's low critical angle (24°) means light undergoes multiple TIRs inside the stone → 'fire' and brilliance. Diamond cutters shape the stone so light enters and undergoes several TIRs before exiting through the top facets. COMPARISON: Glass (n=1.5) → θc ≈ 42°. Water (n=1.33) → θc ≈ 49°. Dense flint glass (n=1.7) → θc ≈ 36°. PATTERN: Higher refractive index → smaller critical angle → more TIR → more sparkling. That's why cubic zirconia (n=2.15, θc≈28°) simulates diamond better than glass. UPSC ANGLE: Diamond geometry and TIR is a classic optics application tested in NDA, UPSC Prelims Paper-1 Science. PYQ FREQUENCY: diamond critical angle in SSC CGL Tier 2, NDA Physics, UPSC Prelims 1× per cycle. MEMORY AID: Higher n = lower θc. Diamond has highest n among gems = lowest θc = most TIRs = most sparkle.

questions.stem: Which of the following medical instruments uses total internal reflection to transmit light?

options.option_text: Endoscope (flexible optical fibres carry light into and images out of body cavities)
Stethoscope (transmits sound, not light, using acoustic tubes) (not this)
Sphygmomanometer (measures blood pressure, no optics involved) (not this)
Electrocardiograph (measures electrical heart signals, no optical fibres)

questions.explanation: ENDOSCOPE uses OPTICAL FIBRES (TIR-based) to: (a) carry light INTO the body cavity. (b) carry the IMAGE BACK to the doctor through separate fibre bundles. Modern endoscopes use a CCD camera at the tip rather than fibre bundles for imaging, but still use optical fibres for illumination. TYPES OF ENDOSCOPES: gastroscope (stomach), colonoscope (colon), bronchoscope (lungs), arthroscope (joints), laparoscope (abdomen — minimally invasive surgery). STETHOSCOPE — purely acoustic, no optics. SPHYGMOMANOMETER — air pressure + mercury column — no optics. ECG — skin electrodes + electrical signal recording — no optics. OTHER TIR-BASED MEDICAL APPLICATIONS: (1) PULSE OXIMETER — uses red/infrared light through finger to measure oxygen saturation. (2) PHOTO-DYNAMIC THERAPY — light-based cancer treatment via optical fibres. UPSC ANGLE: Endoscopy appears in UPSC Science & Technology questions, IBPS GA. PYQ FREQUENCY: endoscope-TIR link in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims, NDA Science 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Light travels from water (n=1.33) to air (n=1.00) at an angle of incidence of 60°. The critical angle for water-air interface is approximately 49°. What happens to the light?

options.option_text: Total internal reflection (60° > 49° critical angle → TIR occurs)
Partial refraction with no reflection (angle too large for Snell's law)
Normal refraction into air (light passes through with bending)
Absorption at the interface (energy converts to heat)

questions.explanation: APPLY TIR CONDITION: Light goes from denser (water, n=1.33) → rarer (air, n=1.00) — condition 1 met. Angle of incidence = 60° > critical angle = 49° — condition 2 met. RESULT: TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION. No light passes into air; all light reflects back into the water. SNELL'S LAW PERSPECTIVE: At the critical angle (49°), the refracted angle = 90° (along the surface). Beyond that, Snell's law gives sin(refraction angle) > 1, which is mathematically impossible — so refraction cannot occur. REAL-WORLD IMPLICATION: Underwater light from below 49° from vertical is trapped inside water by TIR. This is why when looking up from underwater at a shallow angle, you see the bottom of the water (reflected) not the sky. The 'window' for seeing through to air is only within 49° of the vertical — called the SNELL WINDOW. UPSC ANGLE: Submarine periscope optics, underwater sonar environment — UPSC Science & Tech applications. PYQ FREQUENCY: apply TIR condition with given numbers in SSC CGL Tier 2, NDA Physics 1× per cycle. MEMORY: θ incidence > θ critical → TIR; θ incidence < θ critical → refraction.

questions.stem: A glass prism with refracting angle 45° and refractive index 1.5 is used to deflect a ray of light by 90° using total internal reflection. This works because the critical angle of glass (≈42°) is:

options.option_text: Less than 45° (so the 45° incidence inside exceeds θc and TIR occurs)
Greater than 45° (TIR would not occur in this configuration)
Equal to 45° (critical condition — light travels along the surface)
Irrelevant here (prisms work by refraction not TIR) (not this)

questions.explanation: 45° PRISM (right-angle prism) WORKS as follows: Light enters one face perpendicularly (no refraction at entry). Hits the hypotenuse at 45° incidence. Since θc for glass (n=1.5) ≈ 42° < 45° (incidence angle), TIR OCCURS → light reflects at 90°. Exits through the other face perpendicularly (no refraction at exit). TOTAL DEFLECTION = 90°. TWO 45° PRISMS together can create 180° deflection (retroreflector). APPLICATION: PERISCOPES use two 45° prisms (or mirrors) to see over obstacles. SUBMARINE PERISCOPES, BINOCULARS (Porro prism system) use this. CRITICAL CONDITION: If θc > 45° (e.g., if the glass were less dense, n < √2 ≈ 1.41), TIR would NOT occur at 45° and this prism design would fail. At n=1.5 → θc = sin⁻¹(1/1.5) = sin⁻¹(0.667) ≈ 41.8° ≈ 42° < 45° → TIR works. ✓ ADVANTAGE of prism over mirror: TIR is 100% efficient (no partial absorption), while mirrors absorb ~5-10% of light. PYQ FREQUENCY: 45° prism and periscope optics in UPSC Prelims, NDA, SSC CGL Tier 2 Physics 1× per cycle. UPSC ANGLE: military optics, submarine design, binoculars.
